items.reasoning: The title page advertises a description of the country, commodities, people, government and religion — practical knowledge for settlers, not conquest and treasure.
A printed record 'taken faithfully as they were written' by the colony's former governor would reassure and attract settlers and investors.
A 1612 printed book selling Virginia to ordinary English readers shows the shift from exploration voyages to permanent settlement.
Walls, cannons, storehouses, dwellings, gardens — a small fortified post to hold goods and defend the fur trade.
The fur trade needed few settlers and relied on Native partners; a small river post served France better than farms.
One small post on a great river shows France claimed vast territory with very few settlers and had to rely on Native allies and trade.
The text says they 'covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick'.
The Compact lets settlers create government by their own agreement, unlike Spanish rule by a governor sent by the king.
They had arrived and anchored at Cape Cod, outside their patent, so they agreed to govern themselves before going ashore.
The Compact promises government by agreement and says nothing about religious freedom; A, B and C are all contradicted by the text itself (loyal subjects, no rights list, no vote).
'The eyes of all people are upon us' — the world will watch, so they must live up to the godly community.
Winthrop preached it aboard the Arbella in 1630 sailing to found Massachusetts Bay.
The vision claims the world will watch a godly community, but the colony banished Williams and Hutchinson for dissent; B, C and D are not in the stimulus at all.
Table: Spaniards about 350,000 by 1650 — the largest number.
Few, mostly single men — France had to rely on Native partners and allies for the fur trade.
Jamestown: 144 landed, 38 alive a year later, starving time; Massachusetts Bay: 20,000+ families, grew quickly.
The map names Native peoples and towns across the Chesapeake — the settlement stood inside a landscape already named, settled and governed by Native peoples.
A map crowded with names, rivers and resources shows investors and settlers Virginia was known and promising.
The map shows Powhatan society only as Smith understood it from brief visits and secondhand reports — a sourcing limitation.
Fort at the tip, wall, canals, ships in the harbor — a fortified trading port.
A small trading post surrounded by rivals needed defenses more than farmland.
A small company post with few settlers could not mount a defense — the other options are false (a fort and wall are shown; canals did not block ships; religion is not in the plan).
Surveyed parcels each marked with an owner's name — Penn surveyed the land and sold it in parcels.
The regular grid inset shows an orderly, planned capital for the Holy Experiment.
One man held the charter and sold the land, so tolerance served business as well as belief.
Armor, scepter, crown, warships, anchor — a warrior-king ruling by royal authority.
James revoked charters and placed colonies under one royal governor — the crown could rule directly when it chose.
The Dominion collapsed when James fell, so colonial self-government survived a direct royal challenge.
Two men chosen from each settlement met to make laws — the first elected assembly in English America.
An assembly giving settlers a voice in their own laws would attract settlers.
The Burgesses survived the change to royal colony — the habit of elected assemblies was already rooted.
Timber and goods England bought from foreign rivals is the economic argument; faith is the religious one.
Enclosure and population growth left many English people without land or work — the 'idle poor'.
Spreading Protestantism alongside trade = both a commercial venture and a religious-political challenge to Catholic Spain.
Table: Virginia, economic gain (tobacco).

By elimination: A is false (the king did not found every colony), C is false (reasons differ), D is false (Georgia 1732). B is the only defensible answer, though the table itself never names companies, proprietors or religious groups as founders — the founder facts come from the lesson, not the table.
Maryland (Catholics) and Pennsylvania (Quakers) as refuges show the charter system let different religious minorities build their own refuges.
The passage says Georgia was meant as a buffer between Spanish Florida and South Carolina.
Small farmers, not plantations — armed small farmers defending the buffer.
The trustees' design was overturned — colonists' economic interests could overturn a colony's founding design.
The passage says the Acts stayed on the books; what changed was enforcement, not the law.

By elimination: A (independence 1721), B (stopped trading entirely) and C (separate nations) are all false. D is the standard explanation, but the reason is NOT in the stimulus or the lesson — it is outside knowledge.
Decades of self-government made colonists expect it, so post-1763 taxes felt like a broken promise.
Workers hang, press and pack leaves by hand and tend fires — curing took many hands doing skilled work by hand.
Labor-intensive hand work year after year points to a large bound labor force.
The painting shows tobacco curing but not its place (palm trees suggest the Caribbean) or how widespread it was — the lesson itself says its place is unknown.

answer.a: Period 2 Europeans came to stay and planted permanent settlements with families, farms and trading posts, while Period 1 Spain conquered and mined for wealth.
answer.b: The land offered a living: tobacco made Virginia pay, beaver fur made New France pay, and the hope of a godly community drew Puritan families.
answer.c: Native alliances and resistance decided which colonies survived: the French depended on Wendat allies for the fur trade, while Powhatan's peoples fought the English and nearly destroyed Jamestown.

answer.a: Idleness — many Jamestown settlers were gentlemen and adventurers who refused to work, so the colony starved.
answer.b: The settlers came seeking gold and adventure, not farming, but the colony needed farm labor to feed itself — a mismatch between who they were and what the work required.
answer.c: Virginia solved the labor shortage with the headright system and indentured servants, then increasingly with enslaved African labor as tobacco expanded.

answer.a: The map claims the whole eastern region — St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, Labrador, Hudson Bay — as New France or Canada.
answer.b: France claimed a vast territory with few settlers and Native peoples named across it, while England planted dense settler colonies along the coast.
answer.c: The map shows French claims, not control: Native peoples still lived in and controlled the interior, so the map cannot prove who actually governed it.

answer.a: Economic gain — Virginia began as a business venture in tobacco.
answer.b: The profit motive shaped Virginia into a plantation colony growing tobacco on large tracts worked by bound labor.
answer.c: English colonies were founded by companies, proprietors and religious groups, while Spanish colonies were ruled directly by the crown through viceroys.

answer.a: Christians — those professing to believe in Jesus Christ (in practice, Catholics).
answer.b: The Act protected only Christians; it did not protect Jews, atheists or non-Christians.
answer.c: Maryland's leaders passed it to protect the Catholic minority and attract settlers, and to keep religious quarrels from tearing the colony apart.

answer.a: The painting shows the Pilgrims kneeling in prayer on the deck of the Speedwell before sailing in 1620, a Bible open, armor and muskets laid aside, a rainbow over the harbor.
answer.b: It was painted in 1843, more than two centuries after 1620, so it cannot prove what the Pilgrims actually did, wore or looked like.
answer.c: It shows nineteenth-century Americans remembered the Pilgrims as pious, God-fearing founders — the religious origin story of America.

answer.a: France sent few single men who traded furs and built Native alliances; England sent whole families who farmed and pushed Native peoples off the land.
answer.b: Both empires depended on Native peoples at first.
answer.c: The difference came from different goals: the fur trade needed Native partners, while farming settlement needed Native land.

answer.a: Penn claims governments run on the motion men give them, like clocks — made and moved by men, and ruined by them too.
answer.b: Pennsylvania's government gave settlers a real assembly and protected religious freedom, letting the people take part in making the laws.
answer.c: Pennsylvania differed in its religious tolerance: Penn welcomed Quakers, Germans and others while most colonies had an established church.

answer.analysis: Link the examples to the thesis: self-government and family settlement show real difference; dependence on Native peoples and forced labor show real similarity.
answer.complexity: Qualify by region and colony: New England differed most, the Chesapeake shared more with Spanish forced-labor patterns; weigh difference against similarity.
answer.context: Spain built a sixteenth-century empire of conquest and silver; England entered late, after 1588.
answer.evidence_difference: Mayflower Compact, House of Burgesses, family migration to New England; Spanish viceroys and the encomienda.
answer.evidence_similarity: Dependence on Native peoples, forced labor systems, pursuit of wealth through land and trade.
answer.thesis: English colonization differed substantially from Spanish colonization — it was settlement by families and self-governing communities rather than conquest by a crown — but the difference was partial, since both depended on Native peoples and forced labor.

answer.analysis: Explain how the evidence shows the extent: religious conflict directly caused the refuge colonies but not the profit-driven or buffer colonies.
answer.complexity: Religion and profit were intertwined, and the extent differed by colony.
answer.context: England's Reformation, Civil War and Restoration produced the religious divisions that pushed dissenters across the Atlantic.
answer.evidence_other: Virginia's tobacco profits, Carolina's rice trade, Georgia's buffer purpose.
answer.thesis: Religious conflict in England was a major cause of English colonization — it drove the founding of the refuge colonies — but it was not the only cause, since profit and defense drove others.

answer.analysis: Explain how the evidence shows both difference and similarity, linking examples to the thesis.
answer.complexity: Qualify by empire and region: French alliance policy differed most in the fur-trade north, while English displacement was sharpest where farming settlement was densest.
answer.context: Spain built a sixteenth-century empire of conquest; France built a fur trade; England arrived late after 1588.
answer.evidence_difference: The encomienda, the Wendat alliance, English wars of removal.
answer.evidence_similarity: Disease, dependence on Native knowledge, and the taking of land and labor.
answer.thesis: Spanish, French and English treatment of Native peoples differed substantially — conquest, alliance and displacement — but all three empires also shared disease, dependence and land-taking.
